transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2028-06-01 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Ethan Ruiz (Product), Lena Brooks (CTO, Arbor), Samir Patel (Lead ML Eng), Oliver Kim (Platform), Ruth Delgado (Procurement)

---
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll run through a stagewise caching + batching econ lab, show the console, and then map to a pilot that fits your latency budget.
[00:18] Lena: Great, thanks. High level, our main constraint is 50ms p95 for chat responses, cost target is to keep token cost below our current provider by ~30%. We're also strict on data residency and want all inference inside our VPC.
[00:45] Jordan: Perfect. Quick note: we'll touch on Redwwod Console Optimize (transcript sometimes calls it "Redwood Opt"), Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, and then walk a sandbox run. Maya, do you want to kick off the econ model?
[01:05] Maya: Sure. I'll share my screen — okay can you see the cost-sim? (brief pause) I'm showing a baseline: un-cached single-stream at median batch size 1, cost per 1k tokens is the reference. Then we layer in prefix/K V cache hit rates — sorry, transcription typed it K V cache — and batching windows.
[01:30] Samir: Real quick, what's our sessionization assumption? Users have an average session of 6 turns, median prefix length 120 tokens.
[01:38] Maya: We're using the sample histogram you emailed last week — thanks — so the cacheable prefix is typically 80–150 tokens. The econ sim assumes 40% cache hit at first pass, scaling to 70% after warm-up if you use a 30min session TTL and sticky routing.
[01:58] Oliver: When you say sticky routing, that implies session affinity to a GPU pool — does that require Dedicated?
[02:07] Maya: Good question. You can get session affinity on Hosted with our Affinity Gateway but for strict noise isolation and predictable throughput Dedicated pools are recommended. You can stage: start Hosted sandbox for benching, then Dedicated pilot if throughput or SLOs demand.
[02:30] Lena: Can you show a staged rollout plan? We don't want a big bang.
[02:35] Jordan: Yes — that's the 'stagewise' bit. We demo three stages: 1) Local sandbox bench with small sample set and Redwood Optimize console; 2) Canary - 5% of traffic routed to optimized path with KV cache and batching; 3) Full rollout with autoscale and fallback to a smaller model variant if latency spikes.
[03:02] Ruth: From procurement, what documentation do you need before pilot? SOC 2 Type II? SSO?
[03:10] Jordan: We'll send SOC 2 and ISO artifacts; SSO via SAML/SCIM is supported. For Private deployment we support customer KMS/HSM integration and audit logs. We'll attach the security packet after the call.

---
[10:12] Maya: Back to the model: here's a visualization — un-cached token cost is X, with a conservative cache hit of 45% you'd drop per-token compute by ~27% in this workload. If you then increase batching from avg 2 to avg 8 during low-latency tolerant phases, you further reduce marginal token cost but you need a latency budget so we only batch opportunistically.
[10:42] Samir: How do you do opportunistic batching without breaking p95 50ms?
[10:47] Maya: Two levers: adaptive max-wait (we only wait up to 12ms for additional requests at the same model shard) and latency tier routing — requests with strict latency targets can route to a low-batch fast lane (smaller batch size, reserved capacity). The console shows traffic split rules.
[11:20] Jordan: Also prefix caching reduces the work per request since prefix KV cache avoids re-computation of early layers which is the heavy part. That helps reduce the time inside the model kernel too.

---
[20:05] Maya: Now I'm flipping to the console demo. Note the Optimize tab prompts: suggested batch size by qps distribution, cache TTL recommendation, and a cost impact slider that simulates TTL and batch-size tradeoffs.
[20:30] Lena: I like the slider — can we get a simulation that includes intermittent traffic spikes? We have big morning surges.
[20:39] Maya: Yes — you can feed a traffic trace or define a spikiness coefficient. The sim will produce throughput, p95 latency, and estimated cost over 24h.
[21:10] Oliver: If we use Prefix cache, what's the expected memory footprint? Our infra team is tight on GPU ram.
[21:19] Maya: Prefix KV entries are mostly key-value pairs for attention caches. For a 1M active session store, approximate footprint is N * avg-key-bytes * replication factor. In the sim I showed rough numbers: ~12GB per million active sessions under 16k context; but that scales with context and quantization. We'll provide a more exact calc for your sample.

---
[33:40] Samir: We also have to support encrypted KV at rest — will Redwood write to our KMS?
[33:47] Jordan: Yes, for Private deployment we can integrate with your KMS and encrypt in transit and at rest. For Hosted, we have tenant encryption, but integrating customer-managed keys is available on higher tiers.
[34:10] Ruth: Audit logs — how granular are they for compliance?
[34:15] Maya: Token-level tracing isn't stored by default; audit logs capture request metadata, model version, routing decisions, and can include (if you opt in) redacted prompts. We'll send the audit schema in the security packet.

---
[40:02] Maya: Let's step through the staged canary config — here's a sample rollout: 0–5% for 48 hours with increased tracing, compare cost and quality metrics; then 5–25% with autoscale; then full shift if quality reg meets your eval thresholds. We recommend automated rollback on quality regression > X% or latency > 2x SLO.
[40:30] Lena: How do you measure quality degradation for chat? We have several prompt families where hallucinations are sensitive.
[40:40] Maya: Redwood Optimize supports eval sets and prompt-level monitors — you can wire a small automated eval that runs on every canary response (or an offline batch) and triggers alerts. We have built-in regression detection tied to prompt sets.

---
[48:55] Jordan: A quick cost example with numbers specific to your sample mix: baseline monthly tokens 120M. With 50% avg cache hit + batching lift (avg batch 6 during non-peak), model compute cost drops about 42% in the sim. That doesn't include savings from potential quantized model variants which can add another ~15% saving but may slightly affect quality.
[49:18] Samir: Are those savings net of the extra mem and small cache traffic egress cost?
[49:25] Maya: Yes the sim includes KV store cost, small RPC cost for cache retrievals, and additional GPU memory overhead. Net is 42% in our conservative example. We'll deepen the calcs for your actual QPS shape.

---
[55:00] Oliver: For networking, if we do Private VPC, what's the egress model and do we need a direct connect?
[55:08] Jordan: Options: peered VPC or direct express connect, depending on throughput. For high QPS, a private peering with dedicated throughput is recommended. We'll loop infra architects to map ports and NAT.
[55:30] Ruth: Timeline-wise, if we sign pilot Monday, when can we start benching?
[55:36] Jordan: We can stand up a sandbox in 2 business days and run the first bench within a week, assuming your sample dataset arrives.

---
[60:05] Jordan: Quick recap and next steps — agreed pilot, Jordan shares sandbox link and cost sim by 2028-06-03, Maya runs bench and shares raw logs by 2028-06-07, Samir sends prompt mix by 2028-06-05, Oliver confirms VPC constraints by 2028-06-06, Ruth will send PO cadence and vendor forms.
[60:40] Lena: Sounds good. Also please include the rollback runbook and the console guide for canary rules.
[60:48] Jordan: Will do. Thanks everyone.
[61:05] Maya: Thanks, bye.

End transcript. Some words may be transcribed imperfectly (e.g., "KV" as "K V" or "Redwood Dedicate") — we'll attach the raw recording to the ticket for audit if needed.
